questions.q: Which statement is true for a reversible reaction at dynamic equilibrium in a closed system?

options.A: The forward and reverse reactions happen at the same rate, so the concentrations stay constant.
options.B: The concentrations of the reactants and products are equal.
options.C: The forward and reverse reactions have both stopped.
options.D: The reaction has gone to completion in the forward direction.

questions.solution: At dynamic equilibrium both reactions continue, at equal rates, so there is no overall change in the concentrations. The concentrations are constant but almost never equal to each other. (Dynamic means the reactions have not stopped.)

questions.q: For \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_{3}(g)}\), \(\Delta H = -92\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). What happens to the equilibrium yield of ammonia when the temperature is raised at constant pressure?

options.A: It increases, because the rate of the forward reaction increases.
options.B: It is unchanged, because temperature affects only the rate.
options.C: It decreases, because the position of equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction, to the left.
options.D: It increases, because the position of equilibrium shifts to the side with fewer gas molecules.

questions.solution: By Le Chatelier's principle, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction, which opposes the change by absorbing heat. The forward reaction is exothermic, so the position moves to the left and less ammonia is present at equilibrium. (A higher temperature does make equilibrium reached faster, but the yield is lower.)

questions.q: The pressure on the equilibrium \(\mathrm{H_{2}(g) + I_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2HI(g)}\) is increased at constant temperature. What happens to the position of equilibrium?

options.A: It moves to the right, because pressure favours the products.
options.B: It moves to the left, because there are two reactant molecules.
options.C: It moves to the right, because the reaction is faster at higher pressure.
options.D: It does not move, because there are equal numbers of gas molecules on each side.

questions.solution: Pressure shifts an equilibrium towards the side with fewer gas molecules. Here there are 2 molecules of gas on each side, so changing the pressure has no effect on the position (although both rates increase). (Counting the species rather than the gas molecules is the usual slip.)

questions.q: The equilibrium \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}(aq) + 4Cl^{-}(aq) \rightleftharpoons [CuCl_{4}]^{2-}(aq) + 6H_{2}O(l)}\) gives a blue solution on the left and a yellow solution on the right. Water is added to a yellow-green equilibrium mixture. What is seen?

options.A: The solution becomes more blue, because the equilibrium shifts to the left.
options.B: The solution becomes more yellow, because the equilibrium shifts to the right.
options.C: The colour does not change, because water is a product.
options.D: The solution becomes colourless, because the ions are diluted.

questions.solution: Adding water raises the concentration of a product, and dilutes the chloride ions. The equilibrium shifts to the left to oppose the change, forming more \(\mathrm{[Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}}\), so the solution turns blue. (Adding concentrated hydrochloric acid does the opposite and turns it yellow.)

questions.q: A catalyst is added to a reaction mixture at equilibrium. What is the effect?

options.A: The equilibrium shifts to the right, giving more product.
options.B: The rates of the forward and reverse reactions increase equally, so the position of equilibrium is unchanged.
options.C: Only the rate of the forward reaction increases.

questions.solution: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and reverse reactions equally, so both speed up by the same factor. Equilibrium is reached sooner, but its position and the equilibrium constant are unchanged. (A catalyst never improves the equilibrium yield.)

questions.q: The Haber process, \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_{3}(g)}\) (\(\Delta H\) negative), runs at about \(450\ ^{\circ}\text{C}\). Why is a lower temperature not used, even though it would give a higher equilibrium yield?

options.A: At a lower temperature the rate would be too slow, so less ammonia would be made each hour.
options.B: At a lower temperature the reaction would become endothermic.
options.C: The iron catalyst works best at a lower temperature.
options.D: A lower temperature would reduce the pressure, which lowers the yield.

questions.solution: A lower temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction, so the equilibrium yield would be higher, but the rate would be far too slow. About \(450\ ^{\circ}\text{C}\) is a compromise between a reasonable yield and a fast enough rate (the catalyst also needs a high temperature to be active). (The sign of \(\Delta H\) does not depend on temperature in this way.)

questions.q: What is the expression for \(K_{\text{c}}\) for \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_{3}(g)}\)?
questions.solution: \(K_{\text{c}}\) is the product of the equilibrium concentrations of the products, each raised to the power of its coefficient, divided by the same for the reactants: \(K_{\text{c}} = \frac{[\mathrm{NH_{3}}]^{2}}{[\mathrm{N_{2}}][\mathrm{H_{2}}]^{3}}\). (Coefficients are powers, not multipliers, and the reactant terms are multiplied, not added.)

questions.q: What are the units of \(K_{\text{c}}\) for \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_{3}(g)}\)?
questions.solution: \(K_{\text{c}} = \frac{[\mathrm{NH_{3}}]^{2}}{[\mathrm{N_{2}}][\mathrm{H_{2}}]^{3}}\), so the units are \(\frac{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^{2}}{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^{4}} = (\text{mol dm}^{-3})^{-2}\), which is \(\text{mol}^{-2}\ \text{dm}^{6}\). (Inverting the fraction leads to \(\text{mol}^{2}\ \text{dm}^{-6}\).)

questions.q: For \(\mathrm{H_{2}(g) + I_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2HI(g)}\), the equilibrium concentrations at a certain temperature are \([\mathrm{H_{2}}] = 0.0050\), \([\mathrm{I_{2}}] = 0.0020\) and \([\mathrm{HI}] = 0.025\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\). What is the value of \(K_{\text{c}}\)?
questions.solution: \(K_{\text{c}} = \frac{[\mathrm{HI}]^{2}}{[\mathrm{H_{2}}][\mathrm{I_{2}}]} = \frac{0.025^{2}}{0.0050 \times 0.0020} = \frac{6.25 \times 10^{-4}}{1.0 \times 10^{-5}}\) = 62.5, with no units. (Forgetting to square [HI] leads to 2500.)

questions.q: 2.00 mol of ethanoic acid and 1.00 mol of ethanol are mixed with an acid catalyst and left to reach equilibrium: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH + C_{2}H_{5}OH \rightleftharpoons CH_{3}COOC_{2}H_{5} + H_{2}O}\). The equilibrium mixture contains 0.845 mol of ethyl ethanoate. What is the value of \(K_{\text{c}}\)?
questions.solution: At equilibrium: ester 0.845 mol and water 0.845 mol; acid \(2.00 - 0.845 = 1.155\ \text{mol}\); ethanol \(1.00 - 0.845 = 0.155\ \text{mol}\). The volumes cancel, as there are equal numbers of moles on each side. \(K_{\text{c}} = \frac{0.845 \times 0.845}{1.155 \times 0.155} = \frac{0.714}{0.179}\) = 3.99. (Leaving out the water leads to 4.72.)

questions.q: For \(\mathrm{PCl_{5}(g) \rightleftharpoons PCl_{3}(g) + Cl_{2}(g)}\), \(K_{\text{c}} = 0.0400\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) at a certain temperature. An equilibrium mixture has \([\mathrm{PCl_{5}}] = 0.100\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) and equal concentrations of \(\mathrm{PCl_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}}\). What is \([\mathrm{Cl_{2}}]\)?
questions.solution: \(K_{\text{c}} = \frac{[\mathrm{PCl_{3}}][\mathrm{Cl_{2}}]}{[\mathrm{PCl_{5}}]}\). With \([\mathrm{PCl_{3}}] = [\mathrm{Cl_{2}}] = x\): \(x^{2} = 0.0400 \times 0.100 = 0.00400\), so \(x = \sqrt{0.00400}\) = \(0.0632\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\). (Forgetting the square root leads to 0.00400.)

questions.q: The forward reaction of an equilibrium is exothermic. The temperature is increased. What happens to the value of \(K_{\text{c}}\) and to the position of equilibrium?

options.A: \(K_{\text{c}}\) decreases, and the position of equilibrium moves to the left.
options.B: \(K_{\text{c}}\) increases, and the position of equilibrium moves to the right.
options.C: \(K_{\text{c}}\) is unchanged, and the position of equilibrium moves to the left.
options.D: \(K_{\text{c}}\) decreases, and the position of equilibrium moves to the right.

questions.solution: Temperature is the only factor that changes \(K_{\text{c}}\). For an exothermic forward reaction, a higher temperature makes \(K_{\text{c}}\) smaller. The concentrations then adjust to fit the new, smaller value, so the products decrease and the position moves to the left. (\(K_{\text{c}}\) stays the same only for changes in concentration, pressure or catalyst.)

questions.q: More nitrogen is added to the equilibrium \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_{3}(g)}\) at constant temperature. What happens?

options.C: \(K_{\text{c}}\) is unchanged, and the amount of ammonia is unchanged.
options.D: \(K_{\text{c}}\) is unchanged, and more ammonia forms.

questions.solution: \(K_{\text{c}}\) depends only on temperature, so it does not change. Adding nitrogen makes the quotient \(\frac{[\mathrm{NH_{3}}]^{2}}{[\mathrm{N_{2}}][\mathrm{H_{2}}]^{3}}\) smaller than \(K_{\text{c}}\), so the forward reaction makes more ammonia until the quotient equals \(K_{\text{c}}\) again. (The position shifts, but the constant does not.)

questions.q: What is the expression for \(K_{\text{p}}\) for \(\mathrm{2SO_{2}(g) + O_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2SO_{3}(g)}\)?
questions.solution: \(K_{\text{p}}\) uses the equilibrium partial pressures, each raised to the power of its coefficient, products over reactants: \(K_{\text{p}} = \frac{p(\mathrm{SO_{3}})^{2}}{p(\mathrm{SO_{2}})^{2} \times p(\mathrm{O_{2}})}\). (Leaving out the powers is the usual slip.)

questions.q: An equilibrium mixture contains 2.0 mol of nitrogen, 6.0 mol of hydrogen and 2.0 mol of ammonia, at a total pressure of \(250\ \text{kPa}\). What is the partial pressure of hydrogen?
questions.solution: Total amount = 2.0 + 6.0 + 2.0 = 10.0 mol. Mole fraction of hydrogen = \(\frac{6.0}{10.0} = 0.60\). Partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure = \(0.60 \times 250\) = \(150\ \text{kPa}\). (Sharing the pressure equally between three gases leads to 83.3 kPa.)

questions.q: For \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO_{2}(g)}\), an equilibrium mixture at a total pressure of \(100\ \text{kPa}\) has mole fractions of 0.60 for \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}}\) and 0.40 for \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\). What is \(K_{\text{p}}\)?
questions.solution: Partial pressures: \(p(\mathrm{NO_{2}}) = 0.40 \times 100 = 40\ \text{kPa}\); \(p(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}}) = 0.60 \times 100 = 60\ \text{kPa}\). \(K_{\text{p}} = \frac{p(\mathrm{NO_{2}})^{2}}{p(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}})} = \frac{40^{2}}{60}\) = \(26.7\ \text{kPa}\). (Using mole fractions instead of partial pressures leads to 0.267.)

questions.q: For \(\mathrm{PCl_{5}(g) \rightleftharpoons PCl_{3}(g) + Cl_{2}(g)}\), an equilibrium mixture at a total pressure of \(2.00\ \text{atm}\) contains 0.40 mol of \(\mathrm{PCl_{5}}\), 0.30 mol of \(\mathrm{PCl_{3}}\) and 0.30 mol of \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}}\). What is \(K_{\text{p}}\)?
questions.solution: Total amount = 1.00 mol, so the mole fractions are 0.40, 0.30 and 0.30. Partial pressures: \(\mathrm{PCl_{5}}\) 0.80 atm, \(\mathrm{PCl_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}}\) 0.60 atm each. \(K_{\text{p}} = \frac{0.60 \times 0.60}{0.80}\) = \(0.450\ \text{atm}\). (Using the amounts in moles leads to 0.225; inverting the fraction leads to 2.22.)

questions.q: What is the expression for \(K_{\text{p}}\) for the heterogeneous equilibrium \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s) \rightleftharpoons CaO(s) + CO_{2}(g)}\)?
questions.solution: Solids have no partial pressure and their concentrations are constant, so they are left out of \(K_{\text{p}}\) for a heterogeneous equilibrium. Only the gas appears: \(K_{\text{p}} = p(\mathrm{CO_{2}})\), in atm. (Writing the solids in, as for a homogeneous gas reaction, is the usual slip.)
